nodes.name: H-Colouring (homomorphism problem)
nodes.statement: The classical \emph{homomorphism problem}, also known as {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring}, involves a fixed structure~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$, with input another structure~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$, of the same signature, invoking the question as to whether there is a function from the domain of~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ to the domain of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ that is a homomorphism from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Given G, decide whether there is a homomorphism from G to the fixed structure H.

nodes.name: CSP Dichotomy Theorem
nodes.statement: Their well-known conjecture, recently proved by Bulatov~\cite{FVproofBulatov} and Zhuk~\cite{FVproofZhuk}, stated that every CSP$(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ has complexity either in P or \ensuremath{\mathsf{NP}}-complete, omitting any Ladner-like complexities in between.
conclusions: every CSP$(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ has complexity either in P or \ensuremath{\mathsf{NP}}-complete

nodes.name: Surjective H-Colouring
nodes.statement: This paper concerns the computational complexity of the \emph{surjective homomorphism} problem, also known in the literature as {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} \cite{CiE2017,GolovachPS12} and {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Vertex-Compaction} \cite{VikasAlgorithmica}. This problem requires the homomorphism to be surjective.
nodes.statement_short: Decide whether the input graph admits a vertex-surjective homomorphism to H.

nodes.name: H-Compaction
nodes.statement: Indeed, the {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Compaction} problem, hitherto defined only for graphs~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$, takes as input a graph $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ and asks if there exists a function $f$ from $V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$ to $V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ so that for each non-loop edge $(x,y) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ (\mbox{i.e.} with $x\neq y$), there exists $u,v \in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$ so that $f(u)=x$ and $f(v)=y$.
nodes.statement_short: Edge-surjective homomorphism problem: every non-loop edge of H must be covered.

nodes.name: H-Retraction
nodes.statement: The problem {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction} takes as input a superstructure~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ and asks whether there is a homomorphism from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ that is the identity on $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$.

nodes.name: Feder-Vardi equivalence of retraction and CSP classification
nodes.statement: Feder and Vardi~\cite{FederVardi} showed that the task of classifying the complexities of the retraction problems is equivalent to that for the CSPs.
conclusions: the task of classifying the complexities of the retraction problems is equivalent to that for the CSPs

nodes.name: List H-Colouring
nodes.statement: The list homomorphism problem, {\sc List $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-colouring}, allows one to express restricted lists for each of the input structure's elements, that are the only domain elements permitted in a solution homomorphism.

nodes.name: Do Retraction, Compaction and Surjective Colouring coincide?
nodes.statement: At present it is not known whether there is a graph $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ so that {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction}, {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Compaction} and {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} do not have the same complexity up to polynomial time reduction (see~\cite{CiE2017,VikasOther}).
nodes.statement_short: Is there a graph H for which H-Retraction, H-Compaction and Surjective H-Colouring differ in complexity?

nodes.name: Bang-Jensen-Hell-MacGillivray semicomplete dichotomy
nodes.statement: In \cite{Semicomplete} Bang-Jensen, Hell, and MacGillivray proved that {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} is always in \ensuremath{\mathsf{P}}\ or is \ensuremath{\mathsf{NP}}-complete if $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is irreflexive semicomplete.
assumptions: $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is irreflexive semicomplete
conclusions: {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} is always in \ensuremath{\mathsf{P}}\ or is \ensuremath{\mathsf{NP}}-complete

nodes.name: Larose classification of Retraction for reflexive tournaments
nodes.statement: In particular, the classification for {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction} where $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is a reflexive tournament can be inferred from the algebraic characterisation from~\cite{larose2006taylor}: for a reflexive tournament~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$, the {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction} problem is in NL if $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is transitive, and it is \ensuremath{\mathsf{NP}}-complete otherwise.
assumptions: for a reflexive tournament~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$
conclusions: the {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction} problem is in NL if $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is transitive, and it is \ensuremath{\mathsf{NP}}-complete otherwise

nodes.name: $[n]$
nodes.statement: Let $[n]:=\{1,\ldots,n\}$.

nodes.name: neighbour
nodes.statement: In a digraph $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$, a forward- (resp., backward-) \emph{neighbour} (or \emph{adjacent}) to a vertex $u \in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$ is another vertex $v \in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$ so that $(u,v) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$ (resp., $(v,u) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$).

nodes.name: out-degree and in-degree
nodes.statement: The \emph{out-degree} and \emph{in-degree} of a vertex are the number of its forward-neighbours and backward-neighbours, respectively.

nodes.name: isolated vertex
nodes.statement: A vertex with out-degree and in-degree both 0 is said to be \emph{isolated}.

nodes.name: reflexive vertex
nodes.statement: A vertex with a self-loop is \emph{reflexive} and otherwise it is \emph{irreflexive}.

nodes.name: (ir)reflexive digraph
nodes.statement: A digraph is \emph{(ir)reflexive} if all its vertices are (ir)reflexive.

nodes.name: directed path
nodes.statement: The \emph{directed path} on $k$ vertices is the digraph with vertices $u_0,\ldots, u_{k-1}$ and edges $(u_i,u_{i+1})$ for $i=0,\ldots,k-2$.

nodes.name: directed cycle
nodes.statement: The \emph{directed cycle} on $k$ vertices is obtained from the directed path on $k$ vertices after adding the edge $(u_{k-1},u_0)$.

nodes.name: strongly connected
nodes.statement: A digraph $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ is \emph{strongly connected} if for all $u,v \in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$ there is a directed path in $E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$ from $u$ to $v$ (note that we take this to include the situation $u=v$, but for reflexive graphs the distinction is moot).

nodes.name: weakly connected
nodes.statement: A digraph is \emph{weakly connected} if its symmetric closure (underlying undirected graph) is connected.

nodes.name: double-edge
nodes.statement: A \emph{double-edge} in a digraph $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ consists in a pair of distinct vertices $u,v \in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$, so that $(u,v),(v,u) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$.

nodes.name: semicomplete digraph
nodes.statement: A digraph $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ is \emph{semicomplete} if for every two distinct vertices $u$ and $v$, at least one of $(u,v)$, $(v,u)$ belongs to $E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$.

nodes.name: tournament
nodes.statement: A digraph~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ is a \emph{tournament} if for every two distinct vertices $u$ and $v$, exactly one of $(u,v)$, $(v,u)$ belongs to $E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$.
differentia: for every two distinct vertices $u$ and $v$, exactly one of $(u,v)$, $(v,u)$ belongs to $E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$

nodes.name: Tournaments have more than one vertex
nodes.statement: We demand our tournaments have more than one vertex (to rule out certain trivial cases in proofs).

nodes.name: transitive reflexive tournament
nodes.statement: A reflexive tournament $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ is \emph{transitive} if for every triple of vertices $u,v,w$ with $(u,v), (v,w)\in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$, also $(u,w)$ belongs to $E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$.

nodes.name: subgraph
nodes.statement: A digraph~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}$ is a \emph{subgraph} of a digraph $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ if $V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}) \subseteq V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$ and $E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}) \subseteq E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$.

nodes.name: induced subgraph
nodes.statement: It is \emph{induced} if $E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}})$ coincides with $E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$ restricted to pairs containing only vertices of $V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}})$.

nodes.name: subtournament
nodes.statement: A \emph{subtournament} is an induced subgraph of a tournament (note that this is a fortiori a tournament).

nodes.name: All subgraphs are induced
nodes.statement: All subgraphs we consider in this paper will be induced.

nodes.name: homomorphism
nodes.statement: A \emph{homomorphism} from a digraph~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ to a digraph~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is a function $f:V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})\rightarrow V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ so that for all $u,v \in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$ with $(u,v) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$ we have $(f(u),f(v)) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$.

nodes.name: vertex-surjective homomorphism
nodes.statement: We say that $f$ is \emph{(vertex)-surjective} if for every vertex $x\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ there exists a vertex $u\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$ with $f(u)=x$.

nodes.name: homomorphic image
nodes.statement: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ be a digraph. A \emph{homomorphic image} of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is a digraph $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'$ so that there is a surjective homomorphism $h:\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}} \rightarrow \ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'$ in which, for all $(x',y') \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}')$ there exists $(x,y) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ so that $x'=h(x)$ and $y'=h(y)$. That is, $h$ is vertex- and edge-surjective.
nodes.statement_short: Image of H under a vertex- and edge-surjective homomorphism.

nodes.name: direct product
nodes.statement: The \emph{direct product} of two digraphs $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$, denoted $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}} \times \ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$, has vertex set $V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}) \times V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ and edges $((x,y),(x',y'))$ exactly when $(x,x') \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$ and $(y,y') \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$.

nodes.name: polymorphism
nodes.statement: A $k$-ary \emph{polymorphism} of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ is a function $f:\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}^k\rightarrow \ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ so that when $(x_1,y_1),\ldots,$ $(x_k,y_k) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$ then $(f(x_1,\ldots,x_k),f(y_1,\ldots,y_k)) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$. A polymorphism of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ can be seen as a homomorphism from the $k$th (direct) power of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}^k$, to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$.
nodes.statement_short: A k-ary polymorphism is an edge-preserving map G^k -> G, i.e. a homomorphism from the k-th direct power.

nodes.name: idempotent polymorphism
nodes.statement: A polymorphism $f$ is \emph{idempotent} if for all $x\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$, $f(x,\ldots,x)=x$.

nodes.name: essentially unary operation
nodes.statement: A $k$-ary operation $f$ is called \emph{essentially unary} if there exists a unary operation $g$ and $i \in [k]$ so that $f(x_1,\ldots,x_k)=g(x_i)$ for all $(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\in \ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}^k$.

nodes.name: endomorphism
nodes.statement: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ be a digraph. An \emph{endomorphism} of~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ is a homomorphism from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ to itself.

nodes.name: constant map
nodes.statement: An endomorphism~$e$ of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ is a \emph{constant map} if there exists a vertex $v\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$ such that $e(u)=v$ for all $u\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$.

nodes.name: self-map digraph
nodes.statement: The \emph{self-map digraph} $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}}$ has as its vertices the self-maps of $V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$, and there is an edge $(f,g) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$ between self-maps $f$ and $g$ if and only if for every edge $(x,y) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$, we have that $(f(x),g(y)) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$.
nodes.statement_short: Digraph on all self-maps of V(G), with (f,g) an edge iff f and g map every edge (x,y) to an edge (f(x),g(y)).

nodes.name: endomorphism digraph
nodes.statement: The \emph{endomorphism digraph} $\widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}}}$ is the restriction of the self-map digraph $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}}$ to the vertices induced by endomorphisms of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$.

nodes.name: Self-loops of the self-map digraph are the endomorphisms
nodes.statement: Note that the self-loops of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}}$ are precisely the endomorphisms of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$, so $\widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}}}$ is reflexive when $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ is reflexive.
assumptions: $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ is reflexive
conclusions: the self-loops of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}}$ are precisely the endomorphisms of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$
$\widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}}}$ is reflexive

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: The first one follows directly from the definition of $\widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}}}$ as well.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from the definition of the endomorphism digraph.

nodes.name: Composition preserves edges of the endomorphism digraph
nodes.statement: If $(f_1,g_1) \in E(\widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}})$ and $(f_2,g_2) \in E(\widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}})$, then $((f_1 \circ f_2),(g_1 \circ g_2)) \in E(\widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}})$.
assumptions: $(f_1,g_1) \in E(\widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}})$
$(f_2,g_2) \in E(\widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}})$
conclusions: $((f_1 \circ f_2),(g_1 \circ g_2)) \in E(\widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}})$
nodes.label: l-gg2

nodes.name: Currying lemma for the endomorphism digraph
nodes.statement: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ be two digraphs. Let $\varphi$ be a homomorphism from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}\times \ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ to~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$. Then the function $\psi$ defined by $\psi(x)(u)=\varphi(x,u)$ for all $x\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$, $u\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$ is a homomorphism from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ to $\widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}}}$.
assumptions: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ be two digraphs.
Let $\varphi$ be a homomorphism from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}\times \ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ to~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$.
conclusions: the function $\psi$ defined by $\psi(x)(u)=\varphi(x,u)$ for all $x\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$, $u\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$ is a homomorphism from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ to $\widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}}}$
nodes.statement_short: A homomorphism H x G -> G curries to a homomorphism from H into the endomorphism digraph of G.
nodes.label: l-gg3

nodes.name: automorphism
nodes.statement: A bijective endomorphism whose inverse is a homomorphism is an \emph{automorphism}.

nodes.name: non-trivial endomorphism
nodes.statement: An endomorphism is \emph{non-trivial} if it is neither an automorphism nor a constant map.

nodes.name: core
nodes.statement: A digraph, all of whose endomorphisms are automorphisms, is termed a \emph{core}.

nodes.name: fixing a subset or subgraph
nodes.statement: An endomorphism $e$ of a digraph~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ \emph{fixes} a subset $S \subseteq V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ if $e(S)=S$, that is, $e(x)\in S$ for all $x \in S$, and it fixes a subgraph~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}$ of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ if $e(\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}})=\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}$.

nodes.name: retraction
nodes.statement: An endomorphism~$r$ of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ is a \emph{retraction} of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ if $r$ is the identity on the image $r(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$ (thus a retraction must have at least one fixed point).

nodes.name: endo-trivial digraph
nodes.statement: A digraph is \emph{endo-trivial} if all of its endomorphisms are automorphisms or constant maps.
differentia: all of its endomorphisms are automorphisms or constant maps

nodes.name: minimal algebra
nodes.statement: An algebra is called minimal if its unary polynomials are either constants or the permutations (see Definition~2.14 in \cite{HobbyMcKenzie}).
differentia: its unary polynomials are either constants or the permutations

nodes.name: Endo-trivial iff minimal polymorphism algebra
nodes.statement: For reflexive digraphs, polynomials and polymorphisms coincide. In other words, a reflexive digraph is endo-trivial if and only if its associated algebra of polymorphisms is minimal.
assumptions: For reflexive digraphs, polynomials and polymorphisms coincide.
conclusions: a reflexive digraph is endo-trivial if and only if its associated algebra of polymorphisms is minimal

nodes.name: retract-trivial digraph
nodes.statement: A digraph is \emph{retract-trivial} if all of its retractions are the identity or constant maps.
differentia: all of its retractions are the identity or constant maps

nodes.name: term-minimal algebra
nodes.statement: An algebra is term-minimal if the only retractions in its clone of terms are the identity and constants (see~\cite{TermMinimalAlgebras}).

nodes.name: retract-minimal reflexive digraph
nodes.statement: A reflexive digraph is retract-minimal if its associated algebra of polymorphisms is term-minimal.

nodes.name: Retract-minimality equals retract-triviality
nodes.statement: It follows that on reflexive digraphs, the concepts of retract-minimality and retract-triviality coincide.
assumptions: on reflexive digraphs
conclusions: the concepts of retract-minimality and retract-triviality coincide

nodes.name: Endo-trivial implies retract-trivial
nodes.statement: We note that every endo-trivial structure is also retract-trivial.
conclusions: every endo-trivial structure is also retract-trivial

nodes.name: Retract-trivial but not endo-trivial structure
nodes.statement: A tournament on six vertices (self-loops are not drawn), which retracts to the directed 3-cycle (in black) on the right-hand side, but not to the one on the left-hand side (in black as well). However, there is no endomorphism that maps the left-hand one isomorphically to the right. We can use this tournament to build a structure that is a counterexample to the generalisation of Lemma~\ref{lem:endo-retraction-trivial} stating that endo-trivial and retract-trivial coincide. Let us label the vertices in the tournament: $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ (left-hand $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}}^*_3$, clockwise from bottom) and $0,1,2$ (right-hand $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}}^*_3$, clockwise from bottom). Let us build a structure $\ensuremath{\mathrm{B}}$ by augmenting a new $6$-ary relation with tuples in $\{(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,0,1,2),(\alpha,\alpha,\alpha,\alpha,\beta,\gamma),(\alpha,\alpha,\alpha,\alpha,\alpha,\alpha)\}$. The structure~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{B}}$ is retract-trivial but is not endo-trivial, since it has an interesting endomorphism that takes $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,0,1,2)$ to $(\alpha,\alpha,\alpha,\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$.
nodes.statement_short: A six-vertex tournament with an added 6-ary relation gives a structure that is retract-trivial but not endo-trivial.

nodes.name: Endo-trivial iff retract-trivial for reflexive tournaments
nodes.statement: A reflexive tournament is endo-trivial if and only if it is retract-trivial.
assumptions: A reflexive tournament
conclusions: is endo-trivial if and only if it is retract-trivial
nodes.label: lem:endo-retraction-trivial

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3
nodes.statement: (Forwards.) Trivial. (Backwards.) By contraposition, suppose $e$ is a non-trivial endomorphism of a reflexive tournament $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$. Consider $e(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ and build some function $e^{-1}$ from $e(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ by choosing $e^{-1}(y)=x$ if $e(x)=y$ arbitrarily. Since $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is a (reflexive) tournament, $e^{-1}$ is an isomorphism, whereupon $e^{-1} \circ e$ is the identity automorphism when restricted to some subtournament $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$. Hence $e^{-1} \circ e$ is a non-trivial retraction of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ (to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$).
nodes.statement_short: Contrapositive: a non-trivial endomorphism composed with a chosen inverse yields a non-trivial retraction.

nodes.name: Chen's hardness criterion for surjective CSP
nodes.statement: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ be a finite structure whose universe $V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ has size strictly greater than~$1$. If each polymorphism of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is essentially unary, then {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} is \ensuremath{\mathsf{NP}}-complete.
nodes.section: 3 Essential Unarity and a Dichotomy for Reflexive Directed Cycles
assumptions: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ be a finite structure whose universe $V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ has size strictly greater than~$1$.
each polymorphism of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is essentially unary
conclusions: {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} is \ensuremath{\mathsf{NP}}-complete
nodes.label: thm:Chen-hauptsatz

nodes.name: identity map $id_H$
nodes.statement: Let $id_\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ denote the identity map on a digraph~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$.

nodes.name: Maróti-Zádori retraction lemma
nodes.statement: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ be a reflexive digraph. If $(id_\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}},f) \in E(\widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}})$, where $f$ is different from $id_\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$, then $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ has a non-surjective retraction $r$ such that $(id_\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}},r)\in E(\widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}}})$.

$(id_\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}},f) \in E(\widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}})$, where $f$ is different from $id_\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$

nodes.name: Structure of retract-trivial reflexive digraphs
nodes.statement: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ be a retract-trivial reflexive digraph with at least three vertices. Then \begin{enumerate} \item $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ has no double edge; \item $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is strongly connected; and \item the automorphisms of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ are isolated vertices in $\widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}}}$. \end{enumerate}

assumptions: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ be a retract-trivial reflexive digraph with at least three vertices.
conclusions: $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ has no double edge
$\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is strongly connected
the automorphisms of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ are isolated vertices in $\widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}}}$
nodes.statement_short: A retract-trivial reflexive digraph on >=3 vertices has no double edge, is strongly connected, and its automorphisms are isolated in the endomorphism digraph.
nodes.label: lem:Benoit-lemma

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5
nodes.statement: (1) As any reflexive digraph can be retracted onto a double edge, the result follows. \\[3pt] (2) A reflexive digraph that is not weakly connected may be retracted onto a 2-vertex digraph. So we may safely assume $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is weakly connected. If~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is not strongly connected, then $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ has an edge $(a,b)$ such that $a$ and $b$ are in different strong components, that is, there is no directed path from $b$ to $a$. We define a retraction of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ onto the subgraph induced by $\{a,b\}$ as follows: let $r(x) = a$ if there exists a directed path from $x$ to $a$ and $r(x)=b$ otherwise. As $r(a)=a$ and $r(b)=b$, it remains to check if $r$ is an endomorphism. Let $(x,y)$ be an edge. If $r(y)=a$, then there exists a directed path from $y$ to~$a$, and thus a directed path from $x$ to~$a$ implying that $r(a)=a$. If $r(y)=b$, then $r(x)=a$ and $r(x)=b$ are both allowed.\\[3pt] (3) We first prove that no constant map is adjacent to an automorphism in $\widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}}}$. Suppose for a contradiction that there exists an automorphism $\sigma$ backwards-adjacent to some constant (the case of forwards-adjacent is dual). Thus without loss of generality we may assume that $(\sigma,c) \in E(\widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}})$ for some constant map $c$, say for all $u\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$, $c(u)=v$ for some $v\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$. By composing sufficiently many times via Lemma~\ref{l-gg2}, we obtain that $(id_\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}},c) \in E(\widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}})$. Since $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is strongly connected, every vertex $u\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ has out-degree at least~1. Hence $(u,v) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ for all $u \in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$. Since $v$ has out-degree at least~1, this means that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ contains a double edge, contradicting statement~(1). Now suppose that there exists an automorphism $\sigma$ that is backward-adjacent to some endomorphism $f \neq \sigma$ (the case of forwards-adjacent is dual). Thus, without loss of generality we have $(\sigma,f) \in E(\widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}})$. Apply $\sigma^{-1}$ to both sides of the edge to obtain that $(id_\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}},g) \in E(\widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}})$ for some $g \neq id_\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$. By the preceding lemma, and the fact that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is retract-trivial, this means $g$ is a constant map, contradicting the claim above.
nodes.section: 3 Essential Unarity and a Dichotomy for Reflexive Directed Cycles
nodes.statement_short: Each part by exhibiting a non-trivial retraction otherwise. Part (3) uses composition in the endomorphism digraph and the Maróti-Zádori lemma.

nodes.name: Endo-trivial reflexive digraphs have only essentially unary polymorphisms
nodes.statement: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ be an endo-trivial reflexive digraph with at least three vertices. Then every polymorphism of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is essentially unary.
nodes.section: 3 Essential Unarity and a Dichotomy for Reflexive Directed Cycles
assumptions: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ be an endo-trivial reflexive digraph with at least three vertices.
conclusions: every polymorphism of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is essentially unary
nodes.label: cor:Benoit

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement: Since $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is endo-trivial, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is retract-trivial. Hence, by Lemma~\ref{lem:Benoit-lemma}, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is strongly connected, and furthermore the automorphisms of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ are isolated vertices of~$\widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}}}$. As $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is endo-trivial, this means that $\widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}}}$ is the disjoint union of a copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ that corresponds to the constant maps and a set of isolated vertices, one for each automorphism of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$. Suppose for a contradiction that there exists an an $n$-ary polymorphism~$f$ of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ which is not essentially unary. We may without loss of generality assume that~$f$ depends on all of its $n$ variables, where $n \geq 2$. By Lemma~\ref{l-gg3}, the mapping $F:\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^{n-1} \rightarrow \widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}}}$ defined by $F(x_1,\ldots,x_{n-1})(y) = f(x_1,\ldots,x_{n-1},y)$ is a homomorphism. Since $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is strongly connected, so is $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^{n-1}$, and hence so is the image of $F$ in $\widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}}}$. Thus this image is either contained in the component of constants, in which case $f$ does not depend on its last variable, else it is a singleton, in which case $f$ does not depend on any of its first $n-1$ variables.
nodes.section: 3 Essential Unarity and a Dichotomy for Reflexive Directed Cycles
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction: curry a polymorphism into the endomorphism digraph, whose structure (constants copy plus isolated automorphisms) forces non-dependence on variables.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 1
nodes.statement: Combining Theorems~\ref{thm:Chen-hauptsatz} and~\ref{cor:Benoit} yields the main result of this section.
nodes.section: 3 Essential Unarity and a Dichotomy for Reflexive Directed Cycles
nodes.statement_short: Combine Chen's criterion with Theorem 2.

nodes.name: NP-completeness for endo-trivial reflexive digraphs
nodes.statement: If $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is an endo-trivial reflexive digraph on at least three vertices, then {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} is \ensuremath{\mathsf{NP}}-complete.
nodes.section: 3 Essential Unarity and a Dichotomy for Reflexive Directed Cycles
assumptions: $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is an endo-trivial reflexive digraph on at least three vertices
conclusions: {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} is \ensuremath{\mathsf{NP}}-complete
nodes.label: c-main

nodes.name: reflexive directed cycle $DC^*_k$
nodes.statement: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}}^*_k$ denote the reflexive directed cycle on $k$ vertices, which is readily seen to be endo-trivial.

nodes.name: Camion's theorem
nodes.statement: It is well-known that every strongly connected tournament has a directed Hamilton cycle~\cite{Camion59}.
assumptions: every strongly connected tournament
conclusions: has a directed Hamilton cycle

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6
nodes.statement: Hence we derive the following corollary to Lemmas~\ref{lem:endo-retraction-trivial} and~\ref{lem:Benoit-lemma} Part 2.
nodes.statement_short: Endo-trivial gives retract-trivial gives strongly connected; apply Camion's theorem.

nodes.name: Endo-trivial reflexive tournaments are Hamiltonian
nodes.statement: If $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is a reflexive tournament that is endo-trivial, then $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ contains a directed Hamilton cycle.
assumptions: $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is a reflexive tournament that is endo-trivial
conclusions: $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ contains a directed Hamilton cycle
nodes.label: l-Ham

nodes.name: Small homomorphic images have a double edge
nodes.statement: If $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is a reflexive tournament that is endo-trivial, then any homomorphic image of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ of size $1<n<|V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})|$ possesses a double edge.
assumptions: $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is a reflexive tournament that is endo-trivial
conclusions: any homomorphic image of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ of size $1<n<|V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})|$ possesses a double edge
nodes.label: lem:under-m

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 7
nodes.statement: Suppose $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ has a homomorphic image of size $1<n<|V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})|$ without a double edge. By looking at the equivalence classes of vertices identified in the homomorphic image, we can deduce a non-trivial retraction, namely by mapping each of the vertices in an equivalence class to any particular one of them.
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction: a double-edge-free proper image yields a non-trivial retraction via class representatives.

nodes.name: gadget $Cyl^*_m$
nodes.statement: We now introduce the gadget $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$ drawn in Figure~\ref{fig:Photo2}. We take $m$ disjoint copies of the directed $m$-cycle $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$ arranged in a cylindrical fashion so that there is an edge from $i$ in the $j$th copy to $i$ in the $j+1$th copy (drawn in red), and an edge from $i$ in the $j+1$th copy to $i+1$ in the $j$th copy (drawn in green).
nodes.statement_short: m copies of the reflexive directed m-cycle stacked cylindrically, with vertical edges and diagonal back-edges between consecutive copies.

nodes.name: Hamilton cycle $HC_m$
nodes.statement: A key role will be played by Hamilton cycles $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_m$ in a strongly connected reflexive tournament on $m$ vertices. We consider this cycle also labelled $\{1,\ldots,m\}$, in order to attach it to the gadget $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 8
nodes.statement: The following lemma follows from induction on the copies of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$, since a reflexive tournament has no double edges.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on the copies of DC*_m, using that reflexive tournaments have no double edges.

nodes.name: Constant bottom cycle forces constant gadget
nodes.statement: In any homomorphism $h$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$, with bottom cycle $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$, to a reflexive tournament, if $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m})|=1$, then $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m})|=1$.
assumptions: In any homomorphism $h$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$, with bottom cycle $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$, to a reflexive tournament
$|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m})|=1$
conclusions: $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m})|=1$
nodes.label: lem:claim1

nodes.name: Property (dagger) of the gadget
nodes.statement: We will use another property, denoted \textbf{$(\dagger)$}, of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$, which is that the retractions from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$ to its bottom copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$, once propagated through the intermediate copies, induce on the top copy precisely the set of automorphisms of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$. That is, the top copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$ is mapped isomorphically to the bottom copy, and all such isomorphisms may be realised.
conclusions: the retractions from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$ to its bottom copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$, once propagated through the intermediate copies, induce on the top copy precisely the set of automorphisms of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$
nodes.statement_short: Retractions of the gadget onto its bottom cycle induce exactly the automorphisms of DC*_m on the top copy.

nodes.name: Justification of property (dagger)
nodes.statement: The reason is that in such a retraction, the $(j+1)$th copy may either map under the identity to the $j$th copy, or rotate one edge of the cycle clockwise, and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$ consists of sufficiently many (namely $m$) copies of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$.
nodes.statement_short: Each copy maps by identity or a one-step rotation onto the next, and m copies suffice for all rotations.

nodes.name: Spill set $Spill_m(H[H_0,HC_0])$
nodes.statement: Now let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ be a reflexive tournament that contains a subtournament~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ on $m$ vertices that is endo-trivial. By Lemma~\ref{l-Ham}, we find that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ contains at least one directed Hamilton cycle $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0$. Define $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0,\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0])$ as follows. Begin with $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ and add a copy of the gadget $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$, where the bottom copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$ is identified with $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0$, to build a digraph~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0,\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0)$. Now ask, for some $y \in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ whether there is a retraction $r$ of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0,\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0)$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ so that some vertex $x$ in the top copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$ is such that $r(x)=y$. Such vertices $y$ comprise the set $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0,\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0])$.
nodes.statement_short: Glue the gadget onto a Hamilton cycle of an endo-trivial subtournament H_0, forming F(H_0,HC_0); Spill is the set of vertices of H that top-copy vertices can reach under retractions of F to H.

nodes.name: Remark 1
nodes.statement: {\bf Remark~1.} If $x$ belongs to some copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$ that is not the top copy, we can find a vertex~$x'$ in the top copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$ and a retraction $r'$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0,\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0)$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ with $r'(x')=r(x)=y$, namely by letting $r'$ map the vertices of higher copies of~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$ to the image of their corresponding vertex in the copy that contains~$x$. In particular this implies that $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0,\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0])$ contains $V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$.
nodes.statement_short: Any vertex reached from a lower copy can be reached from the top copy; hence Spill contains V(H_0).

nodes.name: Spillage lemma
nodes.statement: If $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is a reflexive tournament that retracts to a subtournament~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ with Hamilton cycle~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0$, then $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0,\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0])=V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$.
assumptions: $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is a reflexive tournament that retracts to a subtournament~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ with Hamilton cycle~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0$
conclusions: $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0,\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0])=V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$
nodes.label: lem:spillage

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 9
nodes.statement: let $y \in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}) \setminus V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$. We need to prove that there exists a retraction~$r$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0,\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0)$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ with $r(x)=y$ for some vertex~$x$ in the top copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$. Let $h$ be a retraction of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$. Suppose $h(y)=i$. We observe that both $(i-1,y)$ and $(y,i+1)$ are edges of $E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$. However, we might have either $(y,i)$ or $(i,y)$ and distinguish between these two cases. First suppose that $(y,i) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$. Then we retract the gadget $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$ associated with $y$ in the following fashion. Using property $(\dagger)$ we turn successive copies of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$ in such a way as necessary to ensure that the vertex directly below $y$ is at position $i$; for a diagrammatic description of what means ``below'', see Figure~\ref{fig:Photo2}. Ih the top copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$ we map the $i$th vertex to $y$ and the $j$th vertex ($j\neq i$) to $j$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$. Now suppose that $(i,y) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$.) Then we retract the gadget $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$ associated with $y$ in the following fashion. Using property $(\dagger)$ we turn successive copies of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$ in such a way as necessary to ensure that the vertex directly below $y$ is at position $i-1$; wherein with the last copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$ we map the $i$th vertex to $y$ and the $j$th vertex ($j\neq i$) to $j$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$. Note that, in both cases, all of the vertices of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$, except one, are mapped to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Case analysis on the edge between y and h(y)=i, rotating gadget copies via (dagger) so the top copy places y.

nodes.name: Base Case I
nodes.statement: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ be a reflexive tournament that retracts to an endo-trivial subtournament $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ with Hamilton cycle $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0$. Assume that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ retracts to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0$ for every isomorphic copy $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0=i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$ of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ with $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0,i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0)])=V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$. Then $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$-{\sc Retraction} can be polynomially reduced to {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring}.
assumptions: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ be a reflexive tournament that retracts to an endo-trivial subtournament $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ with Hamilton cycle $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0$.

Assume that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ retracts to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0$ for every isomorphic copy $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0=i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$ of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ with $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0,i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0)])=V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$.
conclusions: $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$-{\sc Retraction} can be polynomially reduced to {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring}
nodes.statement_short: If H retracts to endo-trivial H_0 and to every full-spill copy of it, then H_0-Retraction reduces to Surjective H-Colouring.
nodes.label: prop:main1

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 10
nodes.statement: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ be an instance of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$-{\sc Retraction}. We build an instance~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$ of {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} in the following fashion. First, take a copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ together with $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ and build $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ by identifying these on the copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ that they both possess as a subgraph. Let $m$ be the size of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ and consider its Hamilton cycle $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0$. We build $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ by augmenting a new copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$ for every vertex $v \in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}') \setminus V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$. Vertex~$v$ is to be identified with any vertex in the top copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$ and the bottom copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$ is to be identified with $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ according to the identity function. See Figure~\ref{f-new} for an example. We claim that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ retracts to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ if and only if there exists a surjective homomorphism from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$. First suppose that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ retracts to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$. Let $h$ be a retraction from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$. We extend $h$ as follows. First we map the copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$ to itself in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ by the identity. This will ensure surjectivity. We then map the various copies of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$. This is always possible: because $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ retracts to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$, we have $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0,\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0])=V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ due to Lemma~\ref{lem:spillage}. Hence, if $h(x)=y$ for two vertices $x\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}')\setminus V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$ and $y\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$, we can always find a retraction of the graph $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0,\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0)$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ that maps $x$ to $y$, and we mimic this retraction on the corresponding subgraph in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$. The crucial observation is that this can be done independently for each vertex in $V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}')\setminus V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$, as two vertices of different copies of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$ are only adjacent if they both belong to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$. This leads to a surjective homomorphism from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$. Now suppose that there exists a surjective homomorphism~$h$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$. If $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|=1$, then by Lemma~\ref{lem:claim1}, $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m})|=1$ for all copies of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$. This means that $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'')|=1$ and $h$ is not surjective, a contradiction. Now, $1<|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|<m$ is not possible either due to Lemma~\ref{lem:under-m}. Thus, $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|=m$ and indeed $h$ maps $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ to a copy of itself in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ which we will call $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0=i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$ for some isomorphism~$i$. We claim that $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0,i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0)]) = V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$. In order to see this, consider a vertex $y\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$. As $h$ is surjective, there exists a vertex~$x\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'')$ with $h(x)=y$. By construction, $x$ belongs to some copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$, and thus also belongs to some copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0,\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0)$. We can extend $i^{-1}$ to an isomorphism from the copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$ (which has $i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0)$ as its bottom cycle) in the graph $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0',i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0))$ to the copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$ (which has $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0$ as its bottom cycle) in the graph $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0,\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0)$. We define a mapping~$r^*$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0',i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0))$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ by $r^*(u)=h\circ i^{-1}(u)$ if $u$ is on the copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0',i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0))$ and $r^*(u)=u$ otherwise. We observe that $r^*(u)=u$ if $u\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0')$ as $h$ coincides with $i$ on $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$. As $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ separates the other vertices of the copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$ from $V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})\setminus V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$, in the sense that removing $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ would disconnect them, this means that $r^*$ is a retraction from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0',i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0))$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$. We find that $r^*$ maps $i(x)$ to $h\circ i^{-1}(i(x))=h(x)=y$. Moreover, as $x$ is in some copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0,\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0)$, we have that $i(x)$ is in some copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0,i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0))$. We may assume without loss of generality that $i(x)$ belongs to the top copy (cf. Remark~1). We conclude that $y$ always belongs to $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0,i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0)])$ (cf. Remark~1). As $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0,i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0)]) = V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$, we find, by assumption of the lemma, that there exists a retraction $r$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0$. Now $i^{-1} \circ r \circ h$ ia the desired retraction of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ to~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduction gluing H and a gadget per vertex; both directions of the equivalence. Key step: show the image copy of H_0 has full spill, then retract.

nodes.name: Tournament with full spill but no retraction
nodes.statement: An interesting tournament $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ on six vertices (self-loops are not drawn). This tournament does not retract to the $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}}^*_3$ on the left-hand side, yet $\mathrm{Spill}_3(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}}^*_3,\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}}_3]) = V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$.

nodes.name: Endomorphisms mapping H_0 to a copy are automorphisms
nodes.statement: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ be a reflexive tournament, containing a subtournament $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ so that any endomorphism of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ that fixes $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ is an automorphism. Then any endomorphism of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ that maps $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ to an isomorphic copy $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0=i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$ of itself is an automorphism of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$.
assumptions: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ be a reflexive tournament, containing a subtournament $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ so that any endomorphism of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ that fixes $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ is an automorphism.
conclusions: any endomorphism of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ that maps $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ to an isomorphic copy $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0=i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$ of itself is an automorphism of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$
nodes.label: lem:7

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 11
nodes.statement: For contradiction, suppose there is an endomorphism $h$ that maps $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ to an isomorphic copy $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0=i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$ of itself that is not an automorphism of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$. In particular, $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})|<|V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})|$. Choose $h^{-1}$ in the following fashion. We let $h^{-1}$ of $h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$ be the natural isomorphism of $h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ (that inverts the isomorphism given by $h$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0$). Otherwise we choose $h^{-1}$ arbitrarily, such that $h^{-1}(y)=x$ only if $h(x)=y$. Since $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is a reflexive tournament, containing precisely one edge between distinct vertices, $h^{-1}$ is an isomorphism. Moreover, $h^{-1} \circ h$ is an endomorphism of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ that fixes $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ and that is not an automorphism, a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction: compose h with a suitably chosen inverse to get a non-automorphic endomorphism fixing H_0.

nodes.name: endo-trivial pair $(H,H_0)$
nodes.statement: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ be an induced subgraph of a digraph $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$. We say that the pair $(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}},\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$ is \emph{endo-trivial} if all endomorphisms of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ that fix $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ are automorphisms.
differentia: all endomorphisms of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ that fix $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ are automorphisms

nodes.name: Base Case II
nodes.statement: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ be a reflexive tournament with a subtournament~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ with Hamilton cycle $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0$ so that $(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}},\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$ and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ are endo-trivial and $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0,\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0]) = V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$. Then $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-{\sc Retraction} can be polynomially reduced to {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring}.
assumptions: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ be a reflexive tournament with a subtournament~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ with Hamilton cycle $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0$ so that $(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}},\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$ and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ are endo-trivial and $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0,\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0]) = V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$.
conclusions: $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-{\sc Retraction} can be polynomially reduced to {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring}
nodes.label: prop:main2

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 12
nodes.statement: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ be an instance of {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction}. We build an instance $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ of {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} in the following fashion. First we build $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ by augmenting a new copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$ for every vertex $v \in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}) \setminus V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$. Vertex~$v$ is to be identified with any vertex in the top copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$ and the bottom copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$ is to be identified with $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ according to the identity function. We claim that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ retracts to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ if and only if there exists a surjective homomorphism from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$. First suppose $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ retracts to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$. Let $r$ be a retraction from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$. Then any extension of~$r$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ is surjective. As $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0,\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0]) = V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ and two vertices in different copies of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$ are only adjacent if both of them are in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$, we can in fact extend $r$ to a surjective homomorphism from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$. Now suppose there exists a surjective homomorphism~$h$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$. If $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|=1$, then Lemma~\ref{lem:claim1} tells us that $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m})|=1$ for all copies of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$, and then we derive $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}')|=1$, contradicting the surjectivity of~$h$. Moreover, $1<|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|<m$ is not possible either due to Lemma~\ref{lem:under-m}. Thus, $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|=m$ and $h$ maps $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ to a copy of itself. As $(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}},\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$ is endo-trivial, Lemma~\ref{lem:7} tells us that the restriction of $h$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is an automorphism of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$, which we call $\alpha$. The required retraction from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is now given by $\alpha^{-1} \circ h$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduction attaching a gadget per vertex; a surjective homomorphism restricts to an automorphism of H by Lemma 11.

nodes.name: Generalised automorphism lemma
nodes.statement: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_2 \supset \ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1 \supset H_0$ be a sequence of strongly connected reflexive tournaments, each one a subtournament of the one before. Suppose that any endomorphism of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1$ that fixes $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ is an automorphism. Then any endomorphism $h$ of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_2$ that maps $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ to an isomorphic copy $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0=i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$ of itself also gives an isomorphic copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1$ in $h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1)$.
assumptions: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_2 \supset \ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1 \supset H_0$ be a sequence of strongly connected reflexive tournaments, each one a subtournament of the one before.
Suppose that any endomorphism of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1$ that fixes $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ is an automorphism.
conclusions: any endomorphism $h$ of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_2$ that maps $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ to an isomorphic copy $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0=i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$ of itself also gives an isomorphic copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1$ in $h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1)$
nodes.label: lem:8

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 13
nodes.statement: For contradiction, suppose there is an endomorphism $h$ of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_2$ that maps $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ to an isomorphic copy $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0=i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$ of itself that does not yield an isomorphic copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1$. In particular, $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1)|<|V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1)|$. We proceed as in the proof of the Lemma~\ref{lem:7}. Choose $h^{-1}$ in the following fashion. We let $h^{-1}$ of $h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$ be the natural isomorphism of $h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ (that inverts the isomorphism given by $h$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0$). Otherwise we choose $h^{-1}$ arbitrarily, such that $h^{-1}(y)=x$ only if $h(x)=y$. Since $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_2$ is a reflexive tournament, $h^{-1}$ is an isomorphism. And $h^{-1} \circ h$ is an endomorphism of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_2$ that fixes $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ that does not yield an isomorphic copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1$ in $h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1)$, a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: As for Lemma 11: by contradiction, composing h with a chosen inverse.

nodes.name: General Case I
nodes.statement: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{0},\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{1}, \ldots, \ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_k, \ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$ be reflexive tournaments, the first $k$ of which have Hamilton cycles $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_{0},\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_{1}, \ldots, \ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_{k}$, respectively, so that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0 \subseteq H_1 \subseteq \cdots \subseteq \ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_k \subseteq \ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}.$ Assume that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$, $(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1,\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$, \ldots, $(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k},\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k-1})$ are endo-trivial and that \[ \begin{array}{lcl} \mathrm{Spill}_{a_0}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0,\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_{0}]) &= &V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1) \\ \mathrm{Spill}_{a_1}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_2[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1,\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_{1}]) &= &V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_2) \\ \hspace*{3mm} \vdots &\vdots &\hspace*{3mm}\vdots \\ \mathrm{Spill}_{a_{k-1}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k-1},\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_{k-1}]) &= &V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_k).\\ \end{array} \] Assume that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$ retracts to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_k$ and also to every isomorphic copy $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_{k}=i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_k)$ of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_k$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$ with $\mathrm{Spill}_{a_k}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_k,i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_{k})]) = V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1})$. Then $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_k$-{\sc Retraction} can be polynomially reduced to {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$-Colouring}.
nodes.statement_short: Chains of endo-trivial pairs with full spills: if H_{k+1} retracts to H_k and every full-spill copy, H_k-Retraction reduces to Surjective H_{k+1}-Colouring.
nodes.label: prop:main-general1

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 14
nodes.statement: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ be an instance of {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_k$-Retraction}. We will build an instance $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$ of {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$-Colouring} in the following fashion. First, take a copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$ together with $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ and build $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ by identifying these on the copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k}$ that they both possess as a subgraph. We now build $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$ as follows. First we augment $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ with a new copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*}_{a_k}$ for every vertex $v\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}')\setminus V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_k)$. Vertex~$v$ is to be identified with any vertex in the top copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}}^*_{a_k}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*}_{a_k}$, and the bottom copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}}^*_{a_k}$ is to be identified with $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_k$ according to the identity function. Then, for each $i \in [k+1]$, and $v \in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{i}) \setminus V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{i-1})$, add a copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*}_{a_{i-1}}$, where $v$ is identified with any vertex in the top copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}}^*_{a_{i-1}}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*}_{a_{i-1}}$ and the bottom copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}}^*_{i-1}$ is to be identified with $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{i-1}$ according to the identity map of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}}^*_{a_{i-1}}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_{i-1}$. We claim that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ retracts to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_k$ if and only if there exists a surjective homomorphism from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$. First suppose that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ retracts to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_k$. Let $h$ be a retraction from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k}$. Extend $h$ mapping $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$ according to the identity to ensure the final mapping is surjective. Finally, we map the various copies of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*}_{a_{i-1}}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$ in any suitable fashion, which will always exist due to our assumptions and the fact that $\mathrm{Spill}_{a_{k}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k},\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_{k}]) = V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1})$, which follows from our assumption that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$ retracts to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_k$ and Lemma~\ref{lem:spillage}. Now suppose that if there exists a surjective homomorphism~$h$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$. Suppose that $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|=1$. Then $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*}_{a_0})|=1$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:claim1}. Now we follow the chain of spills to deduce that $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1})|=1$, which is not possible. Now, $1<|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|<a_0$ is not possible either due to Lemma~\ref{lem:under-m}. Thus, $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|=|V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|$ and indeed $h$ maps $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ to a copy of itself in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$ which we will call $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0=i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$. We now apply Lemma~\ref{lem:8} as well as our assumed endo-trivialities to derive that $h$ in fact maps $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_k$ by the isomorphism $i$ to a copy of itself in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$ which we will call $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_{k}$. Since $h$ is surjective, we can deduce that $\mathrm{Spill}_{a_k}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_k,i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_{k})]) = V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1})$ in the same way as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{prop:main1}. and so there exists a retraction $r$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_k$. Now $i^{-1} \circ r \circ h$ gives the desired retraction of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_k$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduction attaching gadgets along the chain; follow the chain of spills and Lemma 13 to recover a retraction.

nodes.name: General Case II
nodes.statement: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{0},\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{1}, \ldots, \ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_k, \ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$ be reflexive tournaments, the first $k+1$ of which have Hamilton cycles $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_{0},\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_{1}, \ldots, \ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_{k}$, respectively, so that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0 \subseteq H_1 \subseteq \cdots \subseteq \ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_k \subseteq \ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$. Suppose that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$, $(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1,\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$, \ldots, $(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k},\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k-1}), (\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1},\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k})$ are endo-trivial and that \[ \begin{array}{lcl} \mathrm{Spill}_{a_0}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0,\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_{0}]) &= &V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1) \\ \mathrm{Spill}_{a_1}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_2[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1,\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_{1}]) &= &V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_2) \\ \hspace*{3mm} \vdots &\vdots &\hspace*{3mm}\vdots \\ \mathrm{Spill}_{a_{k-1}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k-1},\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_{k-1}]) &= &V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_k)\\ \mathrm{Spill}_{a_{k}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k},\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_{k}]) &= &V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}) \end{array} \] Then {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$-Retraction} can be polynomially reduced to {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$-Colouring}.
nodes.statement_short: Chains of endo-trivial pairs ending at (H_{k+1},H_k) with full spills: H_{k+1}-Retraction reduces to Surjective H_{k+1}-Colouring.
nodes.label: prop:main-general2

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 15
nodes.statement: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ be an instance of {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$-Retraction}. We build an instance $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ of {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$-Colouring} in the following fashion. Build $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ by, for each $i \in [k+1]$, and $v \in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{i}) \setminus V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{i-1})$, adding a copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*}_{a_{i-1}}$, where $v$ is identified with any vertex in the top copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}}^*_{a_{i-1}}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*}_{a_{i-1}}$ and the bottom copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}}^*_{i-1}$ is to be identified with $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{i-1}$ according to the identity map of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}}^*_{a_{i-1}}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_{i-1}$. We claim that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ retracts to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$ if and only if there exists a surjective homomorphism from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$. First suppose that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ retracts to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$. Let $h$ be a retraction from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$. Then we can extend $h$ by mapping $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ in some suitable fashion, which is possible due to the spill assumptions. Now suppose that there exists a surjective homomorphism~$h$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$. Suppose that $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|=1$. Then $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*}_{a_0})|=1$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:claim1}. Now we follow the chain of spills to deduce that $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1})|=1$, a contradiction. Now, $1<|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|<a_0$ is not possible either due to Lemma~\ref{lem:under-m}. Thus, $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|=|V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|$ and indeed $h$ maps $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ to a copy of itself in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$ which we will call $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0=i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$. We now apply Lemma~\ref{lem:8} as well as our assumed endo-trivialities to derive that $h$ in fact maps $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_k$ by the isomorphism $i$ to a copy of itself in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$, which we will call $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_{k}$. Now we can deduce, via Lemma~\ref{lem:7}, that $h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1})$ is an automorphism of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$, which we call $\alpha$. The required retraction from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$ is now given by $\alpha^{-1} \circ h$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduction attaching gadgets along the chain; Lemmas 13 and 11 force an automorphism, whose inverse gives the retraction.

nodes.name: Retraction hardness without Taylor operations
nodes.statement: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ be a finite structure so that the idempotent polymorphisms of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ omit all Taylor operations. Then {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction} is \ensuremath{\mathsf{NP}}-complete.
nodes.section: 4.5 Final Steps for Hardness for Non-Transitive Reflexive Tournaments
assumptions: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ be a finite structure so that the idempotent polymorphisms of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ omit all Taylor operations.
conclusions: {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction} is \ensuremath{\mathsf{NP}}-complete
nodes.label: thm:ret-hardness

nodes.name: Hardness for strongly connected reflexive tournaments
nodes.statement: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ be a strongly connected reflexive tournament. Then {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} is \ensuremath{\mathsf{NP}}-complete.
nodes.section: 4.5 Final Steps for Hardness for Non-Transitive Reflexive Tournaments
assumptions: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ be a strongly connected reflexive tournament.
conclusions: {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} is \ensuremath{\mathsf{NP}}-complete
nodes.label: cor:strongly-connected1

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 3
nodes.statement: As $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is is a strongly connected reflexive tournament, which has more than one vertex by our definition, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is not transitive. Note that {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction} is \ensuremath{\mathsf{NP}}-complete, since non-transitive reflexive tournaments omit Taylor polymorphisms~\cite{larose2006taylor}, following Theorem~\ref{thm:ret-hardness}. Thus, if $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is endo-trivial, the result follows from Lemma~\ref{prop:main1} (note that we could also have used Corollary~\ref{c-main}). Suppose $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is not endo-trivial. Then, by Lemma~\ref{lem:endo-retraction-trivial}, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is not retract-trivial either. This means $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ has a non-trivial retraction to some subtournament~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$. We may assume that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ is endo-trivial, as otherwise we will repeat the argument until we find a retraction from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ to an endo-trivial subtournament. If $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ retracts to all isomorphic copies $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0=i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$ of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ within it, except possibly those for which $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0,i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0)]) \neq V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$, then the result follows from Lemma~\ref{prop:main1}. So there is a copy $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0=i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0)$ to which $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ does not retract for which $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0,i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0)]) = V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$. If $(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}},\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0)$ is endo-trivial, the result follows from Lemma~\ref{prop:main2}. Thus we assume $(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}},\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0)$ is not endo-trivial and we deduce the existence of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0 \subset \ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1 \subset \ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ ($\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1$ is strictly between $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0$) so that $(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1,\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0)$ is endotrivial and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ retracts to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1$. Now we are ready to break out. Either $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ retracts to all isomorphic copies of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_1=i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1)$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$, except possibly for those so that $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_1,i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_1)]) \neq V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$, and we apply Lemma~\ref{prop:main-general1}, or there exists a copy $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_1$, with $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_1,i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_1)]) = V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$, to which it does not retract. Then $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_1$ contains $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}''_0$ a copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}''_0$ so that $(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_1,\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}''_0)$ and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}''_0$ are endo-trivial. We now continue iterating this method, which will terminate because our structures are getting strictly larger.
nodes.section: 4.5 Final Steps for Hardness for Non-Transitive Reflexive Tournaments
nodes.statement_short: Iterate retractions to endo-trivial subtournaments, applying Base and General Cases I/II. Termination since the structures strictly grow.

nodes.name: Hardness for strongly connected tournaments with strongly connected inputs
nodes.statement: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ be a strongly connected reflexive tournament. Then {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} is \ensuremath{\mathsf{NP}}-complete even for strongly connected digraphs.
nodes.section: 4.5 Final Steps for Hardness for Non-Transitive Reflexive Tournaments
assumptions: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ be a strongly connected reflexive tournament.
conclusions: {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} is \ensuremath{\mathsf{NP}}-complete even for strongly connected digraphs
nodes.label: cor:strongly-connected2

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 4
nodes.statement: We need to argue that the instances of {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} that we have constructed before can be assumed to be strongly connected. Noting that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ and the gadgets $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$ are strongly connected, this is clear once we can assume the inputs to our Retraction problems are strongly connected. For {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'$-Retraction}, where $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'$ is a strongly connected reflexive tournament, we can surely assume our inputs are strongly connected. If they were not, then we add individual directed paths of length $|V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}')|$ between the relevant vertices. This will not affect the truth of an instance and the result follows.
nodes.section: 4.5 Final Steps for Hardness for Non-Transitive Reflexive Tournaments
nodes.statement_short: The constructed instances can be made strongly connected by adding directed paths.

nodes.name: standard decomposition of a reflexive tournament
nodes.statement: When $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ is a reflexive tournament, we may break it up into strongly connected components $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}(1),\ldots,\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}(k)$ so that, for all $i < j \in [k]$, for all $x \in \ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}(i)$ and for all $y \in \ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}(j)$, $(x,y) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$. This is the standard decomposition, inducing a standard order on the connected components, that we will use.
nodes.section: 4.5 Final Steps for Hardness for Non-Transitive Reflexive Tournaments
nodes.statement_short: Order the strongly connected components of a reflexive tournament so all edges go from earlier to later components.

nodes.name: Hardness for non-transitive reflexive tournaments
nodes.statement: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ be a non-transitive reflexive tournament. Then {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} is \ensuremath{\mathsf{NP}}-complete.
nodes.section: 4.5 Final Steps for Hardness for Non-Transitive Reflexive Tournaments
assumptions: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ be a non-transitive reflexive tournament.
conclusions: {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} is \ensuremath{\mathsf{NP}}-complete
nodes.label: thm:hauptsatz

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4
nodes.statement: For strongly connected tournaments, the result follows from Corollary~\ref{cor:strongly-connected1}. Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ instead have $k>1$ strongly connected components $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}(1),\ldots,\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}(k)$. Since $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is not transitive, one of these strongly connected components, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}(i)$, must be of size greater than $1$, whereupon we know from Corollary~\ref{cor:strongly-connected2} that {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}(i)$-Colouring} is \ensuremath{\mathsf{NP}}-complete, even when restricted to strongly connected inputs. Let us reduce {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}(i)$-Colouring} to {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} by taking a strongly connected input $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ for the former and building $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ by adding a copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ restricted to $V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}(1)),\ldots,V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}(i-1))$, where every vertex here has an edge to every vertex of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$, and adding a copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ restricted to $V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}(i+1)),\ldots,V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}(k))$, where every vertex there has an edge from every vertex of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$. Note that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ has $k$ strongly connected components $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'(1),\ldots, \ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'(k)$, where $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'(h)$ is isomorphic to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'(h)$ for $h=1,\ldots,k$, $h\neq i$. We claim that there exists a surjective homomorphism from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}(i)$ if and only if there exists a surjective homomorphism from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$. (Forwards.) Map the additional vertices in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ in the obvious fashion (by the ``identity'') to extend a surjective homomorphism from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_i$ so that it is surjective from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$. (Backwards.) In any surjective homomorphism $s$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$, we have that $s(V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'(i))) \subseteq V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}(i))$ for $i=1,\ldots k$.
nodes.section: 4.5 Final Steps for Hardness for Non-Transitive Reflexive Tournaments
nodes.statement_short: Reduce from a non-trivial strong component via the standard decomposition, padding the other components.

nodes.name: Dichotomy for reflexive tournaments
nodes.statement: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ be a reflexive tournament. If $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is transitive, then {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} is in \ensuremath{\mathsf{NL}}; otherwise it is \ensuremath{\mathsf{NP}}-complete.
nodes.section: 4.5 Final Steps for Hardness for Non-Transitive Reflexive Tournaments
assumptions: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ be a reflexive tournament.
conclusions: If $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is transitive, then {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} is in \ensuremath{\mathsf{NL}}
otherwise it is \ensuremath{\mathsf{NP}}-complete
nodes.label: cor:hauptsatz

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 5
