It follows of course that {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} is in \ensuremath{\mathsf{NL}}\ also. The non-transitive case follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:hauptsatz}.
nodes.section: 4.5 Final Steps for Hardness for Non-Transitive Reflexive Tournaments
nodes.statement_short: Transitive case via a median polymorphism and Dalmau-Krokhin; non-transitive case by Theorem 4.

nodes.name: Classification for partially reflexive digraphs on at most three vertices
nodes.statement: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ be a partially reflexive digraph of size at most $3$. Then {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} is polynomially equivalent to {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction}. nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5
nodes.statement: As discussed, we only need to settle the complexity of {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction} and {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} for the digraphs depicted in Figure~\ref{fig:3digraphs}, as for all other partially reflexive digraphs of size at most $3$, {\sc List $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} is in P \cite{FederHellTucker}. When $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is as depicted in Figure~\ref{fig:3digraphs} (a), (c) or (d), then $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is an irreflexive semicomplete digraph with more than one cycle and it is known from \cite{Semicomplete} that {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} is \ensuremath{\mathsf{NP}}-hard, thus the same can be said for both {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction} and {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring}. When $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is the partially reflexive tree of Figure~\ref{fig:3digraphs} (b), {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction} is known to be \ensuremath{\mathsf{NP}}-hard from \cite{pseudoforests} and {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} is known to be \ensuremath{\mathsf{NP}}-hard from \cite{GolovachPS12}. When $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is the reflexive tournament from Figure~\ref{fig:3digraphs} (e), the result follows from Corollary~\ref{c-main} or Lemma~\ref{prop:main1}. For the related case (f), we appeal to Lemma~\ref{lem:case-f} (finishing via Corollary~\ref{c-main}). When $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is as depicted in Figure~\ref{fig:3digraphs} (g), membership in \ensuremath{\mathsf{P}}\ for {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction}, and therefore {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring}, follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:case-g}, in light of the recent groundbreaking proofs of \cite{FVproofBulatov,FVproofZhuk}.

nodes.statement: If~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is the irreflexive directed $3$-cycle, then $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ has a majority polymorphism, which shows that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-{\sc Retraction}, and thus {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} (see Figure~\ref{fig:Anthony}), can be solved in polynomial time~\cite{Semicomplete}.

nodes.name: Which reflexive digraphs are endo-trivial?
nodes.statement: On the way, a natural question arising is exactly which reflexive digraphs are endo-trivial?

nodes.name: Weakening endo-triviality to retract-triviality in Theorem 2
nodes.statement: Finally, there is the question as to whether the assumption of endo-triviality can be weakened to that of retract-triviality in Theorem~\ref{cor:Benoit}.

nodes.name: Claim 0: loops of H^H
nodes.statement: {\em The only loops in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}}$ are the constant maps 1 and 2 and the identity. }
nodes.section: 5 Digraphs with a most three vertices
conclusions: The only loops in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}}$ are the constant maps 1 and 2 and the identity.

nodes.name: Claim 1: edges at constants in H^H
nodes.statement: {\em (a) There are no edges in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}}$ between the identity and the constant maps; (b) if $(2,f), (f,1) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$, then $f=0$; (c) if $c$ is a constant map such that $(f,c),(c,f) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ then $f = c$. }
nodes.section: 5 Digraphs with a most three vertices
nodes.statement_short: No edges between id and constants; a common neighbour pattern of constants 2,1 is 0; a constant's two-way neighbour is itself.

nodes.name: Claim 2: two-way neighbours of the identity
nodes.statement: {\em If $(f,id),(id,f) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ then $f = id$. }
nodes.section: 5 Digraphs with a most three vertices
assumptions: $(f,id),(id,f) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$
conclusions: $f = id$

nodes.name: Forward direction and contrapositive setup
nodes.statement: (Forwards.) Trivial. (Backwards.) By contraposition, suppose $e$ is a non-trivial endomorphism of a reflexive tournament $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$. Consider $e(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ and build some function $e^{-1}$ from $e(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ by choosing $e^{-1}(y)=x$ if $e(x)=y$ arbitrarily.
nodes.statement_short: Forward is trivial; for backward take a non-trivial endomorphism e and a chosen inverse

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Since $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is a (reflexive) tournament, $e^{-1}$ is an isomorphism, whereupon $e^{-1} \circ e$ is the identity automorphism when restricted to some subtournament $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$. Hence $e^{-1} \circ e$ is a non-trivial retraction of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ (to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$).
nodes.statement_short: e^{-1} o e is a non-trivial retraction

nodes.name: Part (1)
nodes.statement: (1) As any reflexive digraph can be retracted onto a double edge, the result follows.
nodes.section: 3 Essential Unarity and a Dichotomy for Reflexive Directed Cycles
nodes.statement_short: A double edge would be a retract

nodes.name: Part (2)
nodes.statement: (2) A reflexive digraph that is not weakly connected may be retracted onto a 2-vertex digraph. So we may safely assume $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is weakly connected. If~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is not strongly connected, then $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ has an edge $(a,b)$ such that $a$ and $b$ are in different strong components, that is, there is no directed path from $b$ to $a$. We define a retraction of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ onto the subgraph induced by $\{a,b\}$ as follows: let $r(x) = a$ if there exists a directed path from $x$ to $a$ and $r(x)=b$ otherwise. As $r(a)=a$ and $r(b)=b$, it remains to check if $r$ is an endomorphism. Let $(x,y)$ be an edge. If $r(y)=a$, then there exists a directed path from $y$ to~$a$, and thus a directed path from $x$ to~$a$ implying that $r(a)=a$. If $r(y)=b$, then $r(x)=a$ and $r(x)=b$ are both allowed.
nodes.section: 3 Essential Unarity and a Dichotomy for Reflexive Directed Cycles
nodes.statement_short: Retract onto an edge across strong components

nodes.name: Reduce to weakly connected
nodes.statement: A reflexive digraph that is not weakly connected may be retracted onto a 2-vertex digraph. So we may safely assume $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is weakly connected.
nodes.section: 3 Essential Unarity and a Dichotomy for Reflexive Directed Cycles
nodes.statement_short: Disconnected digraphs retract to two vertices

nodes.name: Define the retraction
nodes.statement: If~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is not strongly connected, then $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ has an edge $(a,b)$ such that $a$ and $b$ are in different strong components, that is, there is no directed path from $b$ to $a$. We define a retraction of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ onto the subgraph induced by $\{a,b\}$ as follows: let $r(x) = a$ if there exists a directed path from $x$ to $a$ and $r(x)=b$ otherwise.
nodes.section: 3 Essential Unarity and a Dichotomy for Reflexive Directed Cycles
nodes.statement_short: Define r by reachability to a

nodes.name: Check r is an endomorphism
nodes.statement: As $r(a)=a$ and $r(b)=b$, it remains to check if $r$ is an endomorphism. Let $(x,y)$ be an edge. If $r(y)=a$, then there exists a directed path from $y$ to~$a$, and thus a directed path from $x$ to~$a$ implying that $r(a)=a$. If $r(y)=b$, then $r(x)=a$ and $r(x)=b$ are both allowed.
nodes.section: 3 Essential Unarity and a Dichotomy for Reflexive Directed Cycles
nodes.statement_short: Verify edges are preserved

nodes.name: Part (3)
nodes.statement: (3) We first prove that no constant map is adjacent to an automorphism in $\widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}}}$. Suppose for a contradiction that there exists an automorphism $\sigma$ backwards-adjacent to some constant (the case of forwards-adjacent is dual). Thus without loss of generality we may assume that $(\sigma,c) \in E(\widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}})$ for some constant map $c$, say for all $u\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$, $c(u)=v$ for some $v\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$. By composing sufficiently many times via Lemma~\ref{l-gg2}, we obtain that $(id_\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}},c) \in E(\widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}})$. Since $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is strongly connected, every vertex $u\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ has out-degree at least~1. Hence $(u,v) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ for all $u \in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$. Since $v$ has out-degree at least~1, this means that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ contains a double edge, contradicting statement~(1). Now suppose that there exists an automorphism $\sigma$ that is backward-adjacent to some endomorphism $f \neq \sigma$ (the case of forwards-adjacent is dual). Thus, without loss of generality we have $(\sigma,f) \in E(\widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}})$. Apply $\sigma^{-1}$ to both sides of the edge to obtain that $(id_\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}},g) \in E(\widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}})$ for some $g \neq id_\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$. By the preceding lemma, and the fact that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is retract-trivial, this means $g$ is a constant map, contradicting the claim above.
nodes.section: 3 Essential Unarity and a Dichotomy for Reflexive Directed Cycles
nodes.statement_short: Automorphisms have no neighbours in the endomorphism digraph

nodes.name: No constant adjacent to an automorphism
nodes.statement: We first prove that no constant map is adjacent to an automorphism in $\widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}}}$. Suppose for a contradiction that there exists an automorphism $\sigma$ backwards-adjacent to some constant (the case of forwards-adjacent is dual). Thus without loss of generality we may assume that $(\sigma,c) \in E(\widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}})$ for some constant map $c$, say for all $u\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$, $c(u)=v$ for some $v\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$. By composing sufficiently many times via Lemma~\ref{l-gg2}, we obtain that $(id_\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}},c) \in E(\widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}})$. Since $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is strongly connected, every vertex $u\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ has out-degree at least~1. Hence $(u,v) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ for all $u \in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$. Since $v$ has out-degree at least~1, this means that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ contains a double edge, contradicting statement~(1).
nodes.section: 3 Essential Unarity and a Dichotomy for Reflexive Directed Cycles
nodes.statement_short: An id-constant edge would force a double edge

nodes.name: No endomorphism adjacent to an automorphism
nodes.statement: Now suppose that there exists an automorphism $\sigma$ that is backward-adjacent to some endomorphism $f \neq \sigma$ (the case of forwards-adjacent is dual). Thus, without loss of generality we have $(\sigma,f) \in E(\widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}})$. Apply $\sigma^{-1}$ to both sides of the edge to obtain that $(id_\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}},g) \in E(\widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}})$ for some $g \neq id_\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$. By the preceding lemma, and the fact that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is retract-trivial, this means $g$ is a constant map, contradicting the claim above.
nodes.section: 3 Essential Unarity and a Dichotomy for Reflexive Directed Cycles
nodes.statement_short: Apply Maróti-Zádori lemma and retract-triviality

nodes.name: Structure of the endomorphism digraph
nodes.statement: Since $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is endo-trivial, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is retract-trivial. Hence, by Lemma~\ref{lem:Benoit-lemma}, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is strongly connected, and furthermore the automorphisms of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ are isolated vertices of~$\widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}}}$. As $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is endo-trivial, this means that $\widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}}}$ is the disjoint union of a copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ that corresponds to the constant maps and a set of isolated vertices, one for each automorphism of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$.
nodes.section: 3 Essential Unarity and a Dichotomy for Reflexive Directed Cycles
nodes.statement_short: Endomorphism digraph = copy of H plus isolated automorphisms

nodes.name: Assume a non-essentially-unary polymorphism
nodes.statement: Suppose for a contradiction that there exists an an $n$-ary polymorphism~$f$ of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ which is not essentially unary. We may without loss of generality assume that~$f$ depends on all of its $n$ variables, where $n \geq 2$.
nodes.section: 3 Essential Unarity and a Dichotomy for Reflexive Directed Cycles
nodes.statement_short: Take f depending on all n>=2 variables

nodes.name: Curry the polymorphism
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{l-gg3}, the mapping $F:\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^{n-1} \rightarrow \widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}}}$ defined by $F(x_1,\ldots,x_{n-1})(y) = f(x_1,\ldots,x_{n-1},y)$ is a homomorphism.
nodes.section: 3 Essential Unarity and a Dichotomy for Reflexive Directed Cycles
nodes.statement_short: F: H^{n-1} -> endomorphism digraph is a homomorphism

nodes.name: Image is strongly connected
nodes.statement: Since $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is strongly connected, so is $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^{n-1}$, and hence so is the image of $F$ in $\widehat{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}}}$.
nodes.section: 3 Essential Unarity and a Dichotomy for Reflexive Directed Cycles
nodes.statement_short: Strong connectivity passes to the image of F

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Thus this image is either contained in the component of constants, in which case $f$ does not depend on its last variable, else it is a singleton, in which case $f$ does not depend on any of its first $n-1$ variables.
nodes.section: 3 Essential Unarity and a Dichotomy for Reflexive Directed Cycles
nodes.statement_short: Image in constants or a singleton contradicts dependence

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement: let $y \in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}) \setminus V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$. We need to prove that there exists a retraction~$r$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0,\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0)$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ with $r(x)=y$ for some vertex~$x$ in the top copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix y outside H_0 and state the required retraction

nodes.name: Use the retraction to H_0
nodes.statement: Let $h$ be a retraction of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$. Suppose $h(y)=i$. We observe that both $(i-1,y)$ and $(y,i+1)$ are edges of $E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$. However, we might have either $(y,i)$ or $(i,y)$ and distinguish between these two cases.
nodes.statement_short: With h(y)=i, y lies between i-1 and i+1

nodes.name: Case (y,i) edge
nodes.statement: First suppose that $(y,i) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$. Then we retract the gadget $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$ associated with $y$ in the following fashion. Using property $(\dagger)$ we turn successive copies of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$ in such a way as necessary to ensure that the vertex directly below $y$ is at position $i$; for a diagrammatic description of what means ``below'', see Figure~\ref{fig:Photo2}. Ih the top copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$ we map the $i$th vertex to $y$ and the $j$th vertex ($j\neq i$) to $j$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Rotate copies so y sits above position i

nodes.name: Case (i,y) edge
nodes.statement: Now suppose that $(i,y) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$.) Then we retract the gadget $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$ associated with $y$ in the following fashion. Using property $(\dagger)$ we turn successive copies of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$ in such a way as necessary to ensure that the vertex directly below $y$ is at position $i-1$; wherein with the last copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$ we map the $i$th vertex to $y$ and the $j$th vertex ($j\neq i$) to $j$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Rotate copies so y sits above position i-1

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Note that, in both cases, all of the vertices of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$, except one, are mapped to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$.
nodes.statement_short: All but one gadget vertex map into H_0

nodes.name: Construct the instance
nodes.statement: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ be an instance of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$-{\sc Retraction}. We build an instance~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$ of {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} in the following fashion. First, take a copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ together with $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ and build $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ by identifying these on the copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ that they both possess as a subgraph. Let $m$ be the size of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ and consider its Hamilton cycle $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0$. We build $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ by augmenting a new copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$ for every vertex $v \in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}') \setminus V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$. Vertex~$v$ is to be identified with any vertex in the top copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$ and the bottom copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$ is to be identified with $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ according to the identity function. See Figure~\ref{f-new} for an example.
nodes.statement_short: Glue H to G on H_0 and attach a gadget per extra vertex

nodes.name: State the equivalence
nodes.statement: We claim that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ retracts to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ if and only if there exists a surjective homomorphism from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$.
nodes.statement_short: G retracts to H_0 iff G'' maps surjectively to H

nodes.name: Forward direction
nodes.statement: First suppose that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ retracts to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$. Let $h$ be a retraction from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$. We extend $h$ as follows. First we map the copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$ to itself in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ by the identity. This will ensure surjectivity. We then map the various copies of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$. This is always possible: because $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ retracts to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$, we have $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0,\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0])=V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ due to Lemma~\ref{lem:spillage}. Hence, if $h(x)=y$ for two vertices $x\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}')\setminus V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$ and $y\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$, we can always find a retraction of the graph $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0,\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0)$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ that maps $x$ to $y$, and we mimic this retraction on the corresponding subgraph in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$. The crucial observation is that this can be done independently for each vertex in $V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}')\setminus V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$, as two vertices of different copies of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$ are only adjacent if they both belong to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$. This leads to a surjective homomorphism from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Extend a retraction gadget-wise using full spill (Lemma 9)

nodes.name: Backward direction: H_0 maps isomorphically
nodes.statement: Now suppose that there exists a surjective homomorphism~$h$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$. If $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|=1$, then by Lemma~\ref{lem:claim1}, $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m})|=1$ for all copies of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$. This means that $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'')|=1$ and $h$ is not surjective, a contradiction. Now, $1<|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|<m$ is not possible either due to Lemma~\ref{lem:under-m}. Thus, $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|=m$ and indeed $h$ maps $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ to a copy of itself in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ which we will call $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0=i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$ for some isomorphism~$i$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemmas 8 and 7 force |h(H_0)|=m

nodes.name: Claim: full spill of the image copy
nodes.statement: We claim that $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0,i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0)]) = V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$. In order to see this, consider a vertex $y\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$. As $h$ is surjective, there exists a vertex~$x\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'')$ with $h(x)=y$. By construction, $x$ belongs to some copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$, and thus also belongs to some copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0,\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0)$. We can extend $i^{-1}$ to an isomorphism from the copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$ (which has $i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0)$ as its bottom cycle) in the graph $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0',i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0))$ to the copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$ (which has $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0$ as its bottom cycle) in the graph $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0,\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0)$. We define a mapping~$r^*$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0',i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0))$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ by $r^*(u)=h\circ i^{-1}(u)$ if $u$ is on the copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0',i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0))$ and $r^*(u)=u$ otherwise. We observe that $r^*(u)=u$ if $u\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0')$ as $h$ coincides with $i$ on $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$. As $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ separates the other vertices of the copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$ from $V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})\setminus V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$, in the sense that removing $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ would disconnect them, this means that $r^*$ is a retraction from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0',i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0))$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$. We find that $r^*$ maps $i(x)$ to $h\circ i^{-1}(i(x))=h(x)=y$. Moreover, as $x$ is in some copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0,\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0)$, we have that $i(x)$ is in some copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0,i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0))$. We may assume without loss of generality that $i(x)$ belongs to the top copy (cf. Remark~1). We conclude that $y$ always belongs to $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0,i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0)])$ (cf. Remark~1).
nodes.statement_short: The image copy of H_0 has full spill

nodes.name: Pick a preimage
nodes.statement: As $h$ is surjective, there exists a vertex~$x\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'')$ with $h(x)=y$. By construction, $x$ belongs to some copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$, and thus also belongs to some copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0,\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0)$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose x with h(x)=y lying in a gadget copy

nodes.name: Build retraction r*
nodes.statement: We can extend $i^{-1}$ to an isomorphism from the copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$ (which has $i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0)$ as its bottom cycle) in the graph $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0',i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0))$ to the copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$ (which has $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0$ as its bottom cycle) in the graph $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0,\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0)$. We define a mapping~$r^*$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0',i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0))$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ by $r^*(u)=h\circ i^{-1}(u)$ if $u$ is on the copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0',i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0))$ and $r^*(u)=u$ otherwise. We observe that $r^*(u)=u$ if $u\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0')$ as $h$ coincides with $i$ on $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$. As $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ separates the other vertices of the copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$ from $V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})\setminus V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$, in the sense that removing $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ would disconnect them, this means that $r^*$ is a retraction from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0',i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0))$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Transport h along i^{-1} to a retraction r*

nodes.name: Conclude claim
nodes.statement: We find that $r^*$ maps $i(x)$ to $h\circ i^{-1}(i(x))=h(x)=y$. Moreover, as $x$ is in some copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0,\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0)$, we have that $i(x)$ is in some copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0,i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0))$. We may assume without loss of generality that $i(x)$ belongs to the top copy (cf. Remark~1). We conclude that $y$ always belongs to $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0,i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0)])$ (cf. Remark~1).
nodes.statement_short: r* sends i(x) to y, so y is in the spill

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: As $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0,i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0)]) = V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$, we find, by assumption of the lemma, that there exists a retraction $r$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0$. Now $i^{-1} \circ r \circ h$ ia the desired retraction of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ to~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the hypothesis to retract and compose

nodes.name: Assume a counterexample
nodes.statement: For contradiction, suppose there is an endomorphism $h$ that maps $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ to an isomorphic copy $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0=i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$ of itself that is not an automorphism of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$. In particular, $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})|<|V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})|$.
nodes.statement_short: h maps H_0 to a copy but is not an automorphism

nodes.name: Choose an inverse
nodes.statement: Choose $h^{-1}$ in the following fashion. We let $h^{-1}$ of $h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$ be the natural isomorphism of $h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ (that inverts the isomorphism given by $h$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0$). Otherwise we choose $h^{-1}$ arbitrarily, such that $h^{-1}(y)=x$ only if $h(x)=y$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick h^{-1} inverting h on H_0

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Since $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is a reflexive tournament, containing precisely one edge between distinct vertices, $h^{-1}$ is an isomorphism. Moreover, $h^{-1} \circ h$ is an endomorphism of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ that fixes $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ and that is not an automorphism, a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: h^{-1} o h fixes H_0 but is not an automorphism

nodes.name: Construct the instance
nodes.statement: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ be an instance of {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction}. We build an instance $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ of {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} in the following fashion. First we build $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ by augmenting a new copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$ for every vertex $v \in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}) \setminus V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$. Vertex~$v$ is to be identified with any vertex in the top copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$ and the bottom copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}^*_m}$ is to be identified with $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ according to the identity function.
nodes.statement_short: Attach a gadget per vertex outside H_0

nodes.name: State the equivalence
nodes.statement: We claim that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ retracts to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ if and only if there exists a surjective homomorphism from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$.
nodes.statement_short: G retracts to H iff G' maps surjectively to H

nodes.name: Forward direction
nodes.statement: First suppose $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ retracts to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$. Let $r$ be a retraction from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$. Then any extension of~$r$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ is surjective. As $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0,\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0]) = V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ and two vertices in different copies of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$ are only adjacent if both of them are in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$, we can in fact extend $r$ to a surjective homomorphism from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Extend a retraction using full spill

nodes.name: Backward direction
nodes.statement: Now suppose there exists a surjective homomorphism~$h$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$. If $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|=1$, then Lemma~\ref{lem:claim1} tells us that $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m})|=1$ for all copies of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$, and then we derive $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}')|=1$, contradicting the surjectivity of~$h$. Moreover, $1<|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|<m$ is not possible either due to Lemma~\ref{lem:under-m}. Thus, $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|=m$ and $h$ maps $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ to a copy of itself. As $(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}},\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$ is endo-trivial, Lemma~\ref{lem:7} tells us that the restriction of $h$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is an automorphism of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$, which we call $\alpha$. The required retraction from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is now given by $\alpha^{-1} \circ h$.
nodes.statement_short: H_0 maps isomorphically; Lemma 11 gives an automorphism alpha

nodes.name: Assume a counterexample
nodes.statement: For contradiction, suppose there is an endomorphism $h$ of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_2$ that maps $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ to an isomorphic copy $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0=i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$ of itself that does not yield an isomorphic copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1$. In particular, $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1)|<|V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1)|$.
nodes.statement_short: h shrinks H_1

nodes.name: Follow Lemma 11
nodes.statement: We proceed as in the proof of the Lemma~\ref{lem:7}.
nodes.statement_short: Same argument as Lemma 11

nodes.name: Choose an inverse
nodes.statement: Choose $h^{-1}$ in the following fashion. We let $h^{-1}$ of $h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$ be the natural isomorphism of $h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ (that inverts the isomorphism given by $h$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0$). Otherwise we choose $h^{-1}$ arbitrarily, such that $h^{-1}(y)=x$ only if $h(x)=y$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick h^{-1} inverting h on H_0

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Since $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_2$ is a reflexive tournament, $h^{-1}$ is an isomorphism. And $h^{-1} \circ h$ is an endomorphism of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_2$ that fixes $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ that does not yield an isomorphic copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1$ in $h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1)$, a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: h^{-1} o h fixes H_0 but collapses H_1

nodes.name: Construct the instance
nodes.statement: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ be an instance of {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_k$-Retraction}. We will build an instance $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$ of {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$-Colouring} in the following fashion. First, take a copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$ together with $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ and build $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ by identifying these on the copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k}$ that they both possess as a subgraph. We now build $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$ as follows. First we augment $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ with a new copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*}_{a_k}$ for every vertex $v\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}')\setminus V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_k)$. Vertex~$v$ is to be identified with any vertex in the top copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}}^*_{a_k}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*}_{a_k}$, and the bottom copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}}^*_{a_k}$ is to be identified with $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_k$ according to the identity function. Then, for each $i \in [k+1]$, and $v \in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{i}) \setminus V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{i-1})$, add a copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*}_{a_{i-1}}$, where $v$ is identified with any vertex in the top copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}}^*_{a_{i-1}}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*}_{a_{i-1}}$ and the bottom copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}}^*_{i-1}$ is to be identified with $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{i-1}$ according to the identity map of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}}^*_{a_{i-1}}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_{i-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Glue H_{k+1} to G and attach gadgets along the chain

nodes.name: State the equivalence
nodes.statement: We claim that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ retracts to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_k$ if and only if there exists a surjective homomorphism from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$.
nodes.statement_short: G retracts to H_k iff G'' maps surjectively to H_{k+1}

nodes.name: Forward direction
nodes.statement: First suppose that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ retracts to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_k$. Let $h$ be a retraction from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k}$. Extend $h$ mapping $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$ according to the identity to ensure the final mapping is surjective. Finally, we map the various copies of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*}_{a_{i-1}}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$ in any suitable fashion, which will always exist due to our assumptions and the fact that $\mathrm{Spill}_{a_{k}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k},\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_{k}]) = V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1})$, which follows from our assumption that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$ retracts to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_k$ and Lemma~\ref{lem:spillage}.
nodes.statement_short: Extend the retraction using spill assumptions and Lemma 9

nodes.name: Backward direction
nodes.statement: Now suppose that if there exists a surjective homomorphism~$h$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$. Suppose that $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|=1$. Then $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*}_{a_0})|=1$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:claim1}. Now we follow the chain of spills to deduce that $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1})|=1$, which is not possible. Now, $1<|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|<a_0$ is not possible either due to Lemma~\ref{lem:under-m}. Thus, $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|=|V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|$ and indeed $h$ maps $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ to a copy of itself in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$ which we will call $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0=i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$. We now apply Lemma~\ref{lem:8} as well as our assumed endo-trivialities to derive that $h$ in fact maps $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_k$ by the isomorphism $i$ to a copy of itself in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$ which we will call $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_{k}$. Since $h$ is surjective, we can deduce that $\mathrm{Spill}_{a_k}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_k,i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_{k})]) = V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1})$ in the same way as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{prop:main1}. and so there exists a retraction $r$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_k$. Now $i^{-1} \circ r \circ h$ gives the desired retraction of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_k$.
nodes.statement_short: Chain of spills, Lemmas 7, 8, 13 give a retraction

nodes.name: Construct the instance
nodes.statement: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ be an instance of {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$-Retraction}. We build an instance $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ of {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$-Colouring} in the following fashion. Build $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ by, for each $i \in [k+1]$, and $v \in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{i}) \setminus V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{i-1})$, adding a copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*}_{a_{i-1}}$, where $v$ is identified with any vertex in the top copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}}^*_{a_{i-1}}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*}_{a_{i-1}}$ and the bottom copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}}^*_{i-1}$ is to be identified with $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{i-1}$ according to the identity map of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{DC}}^*_{a_{i-1}}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_{i-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Attach gadgets along the chain

nodes.name: State the equivalence
nodes.statement: We claim that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ retracts to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$ if and only if there exists a surjective homomorphism from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$.
nodes.statement_short: G retracts to H_{k+1} iff G' maps surjectively

nodes.name: Forward direction
nodes.statement: First suppose that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ retracts to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$. Let $h$ be a retraction from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$. Then we can extend $h$ by mapping $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ in some suitable fashion, which is possible due to the spill assumptions.
nodes.statement_short: Extend via spill assumptions

nodes.name: Backward direction
nodes.statement: Now suppose that there exists a surjective homomorphism~$h$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$. Suppose that $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|=1$. Then $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*}_{a_0})|=1$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:claim1}. Now we follow the chain of spills to deduce that $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1})|=1$, a contradiction. Now, $1<|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|<a_0$ is not possible either due to Lemma~\ref{lem:under-m}. Thus, $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|=|V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|$ and indeed $h$ maps $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ to a copy of itself in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$ which we will call $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0=i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$. We now apply Lemma~\ref{lem:8} as well as our assumed endo-trivialities to derive that $h$ in fact maps $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_k$ by the isomorphism $i$ to a copy of itself in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$, which we will call $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_{k}$. Now we can deduce, via Lemma~\ref{lem:7}, that $h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1})$ is an automorphism of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$, which we call $\alpha$. The required retraction from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_{k+1}$ is now given by $\alpha^{-1} \circ h$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemmas 7, 8, 13, 11 yield an automorphism alpha

nodes.name: H is not transitive
nodes.statement: As $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is is a strongly connected reflexive tournament, which has more than one vertex by our definition, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is not transitive.
nodes.section: 4.5 Final Steps for Hardness for Non-Transitive Reflexive Tournaments
nodes.statement_short: Strongly connected with >1 vertex means non-transitive

nodes.name: Retraction is NP-complete
nodes.statement: Note that {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction} is \ensuremath{\mathsf{NP}}-complete, since non-transitive reflexive tournaments omit Taylor polymorphisms~\cite{larose2006taylor}, following Theorem~\ref{thm:ret-hardness}.
nodes.section: 4.5 Final Steps for Hardness for Non-Transitive Reflexive Tournaments
nodes.statement_short: Non-transitive tournaments omit Taylor polymorphisms

nodes.name: Endo-trivial case
nodes.statement: Thus, if $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is endo-trivial, the result follows from Lemma~\ref{prop:main1} (note that we could also have used Corollary~\ref{c-main}).
nodes.section: 4.5 Final Steps for Hardness for Non-Transitive Reflexive Tournaments
nodes.statement_short: Apply Base Case I

nodes.name: Non-endo-trivial case
nodes.statement: Suppose $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is not endo-trivial. Then, by Lemma~\ref{lem:endo-retraction-trivial}, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is not retract-trivial either. This means $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ has a non-trivial retraction to some subtournament~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$. We may assume that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ is endo-trivial, as otherwise we will repeat the argument until we find a retraction from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ to an endo-trivial subtournament.
nodes.section: 4.5 Final Steps for Hardness for Non-Transitive Reflexive Tournaments
nodes.statement_short: Retract to an endo-trivial subtournament H_0

nodes.name: Iterate the base and general cases
nodes.statement: If $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ retracts to all isomorphic copies $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0=i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$ of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ within it, except possibly those for which $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0,i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0)]) \neq V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$, then the result follows from Lemma~\ref{prop:main1}. So there is a copy $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0=i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0)$ to which $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ does not retract for which $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0,i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_0)]) = V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$. If $(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}},\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0)$ is endo-trivial, the result follows from Lemma~\ref{prop:main2}. Thus we assume $(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}},\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0)$ is not endo-trivial and we deduce the existence of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0 \subset \ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1 \subset \ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ ($\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1$ is strictly between $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0$) so that $(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1,\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0)$ is endotrivial and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ retracts to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1$. Now we are ready to break out. Either $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ retracts to all isomorphic copies of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_1=i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_1)$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$, except possibly for those so that $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_1,i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_1)]) \neq V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$, and we apply Lemma~\ref{prop:main-general1}, or there exists a copy $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_1$, with $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_1,i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{HC}}_1)]) = V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$, to which it does not retract. Then $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_1$ contains $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}''_0$ a copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}''_0$ so that $(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_1,\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}''_0)$ and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}''_0$ are endo-trivial. We now continue iterating this method, which will terminate because our structures are getting strictly larger.
nodes.section: 4.5 Final Steps for Hardness for Non-Transitive Reflexive Tournaments
nodes.statement_short: Apply Base/General Cases, building larger endo-trivial pairs until done

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement: We need to argue that the instances of {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} that we have constructed before can be assumed to be strongly connected.
nodes.section: 4.5 Final Steps for Hardness for Non-Transitive Reflexive Tournaments
nodes.statement_short: Instances must be strongly connected

nodes.name: Reduce to inputs
nodes.statement: Noting that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ and the gadgets $\ensuremath{\mathrm{Cyl}^*_m}$ are strongly connected, this is clear once we can assume the inputs to our Retraction problems are strongly connected.
nodes.section: 4.5 Final Steps for Hardness for Non-Transitive Reflexive Tournaments
nodes.statement_short: Suffices that Retraction inputs are strongly connected

nodes.name: Make inputs strongly connected
nodes.statement: For {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'$-Retraction}, where $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'$ is a strongly connected reflexive tournament, we can surely assume our inputs are strongly connected. If they were not, then we add individual directed paths of length $|V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}')|$ between the relevant vertices. This will not affect the truth of an instance and the result follows.
nodes.section: 4.5 Final Steps for Hardness for Non-Transitive Reflexive Tournaments
nodes.statement_short: Add directed paths between vertices

nodes.name: Strongly connected case
nodes.statement: For strongly connected tournaments, the result follows from Corollary~\ref{cor:strongly-connected1}.
nodes.section: 4.5 Final Steps for Hardness for Non-Transitive Reflexive Tournaments
nodes.statement_short: Corollary 3

nodes.name: Several components
nodes.statement: Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ instead have $k>1$ strongly connected components $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}(1),\ldots,\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}(k)$. Since $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is not transitive, one of these strongly connected components, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}(i)$, must be of size greater than $1$, whereupon we know from Corollary~\ref{cor:strongly-connected2} that {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}(i)$-Colouring} is \ensuremath{\mathsf{NP}}-complete, even when restricted to strongly connected inputs.
nodes.section: 4.5 Final Steps for Hardness for Non-Transitive Reflexive Tournaments
nodes.statement_short: Some component H(i) is non-trivial, hard by Corollary 4

nodes.name: Construct the reduction
nodes.statement: Let us reduce {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}(i)$-Colouring} to {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} by taking a strongly connected input $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ for the former and building $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ by adding a copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ restricted to $V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}(1)),\ldots,V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}(i-1))$, where every vertex here has an edge to every vertex of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$, and adding a copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ restricted to $V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}(i+1)),\ldots,V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}(k))$, where every vertex there has an edge from every vertex of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$. Note that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ has $k$ strongly connected components $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'(1),\ldots, \ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'(k)$, where $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'(h)$ is isomorphic to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'(h)$ for $h=1,\ldots,k$, $h\neq i$.
nodes.section: 4.5 Final Steps for Hardness for Non-Transitive Reflexive Tournaments
nodes.statement_short: Pad G with the other components of H

nodes.name: State the equivalence
nodes.statement: We claim that there exists a surjective homomorphism from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}(i)$ if and only if there exists a surjective homomorphism from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$.
nodes.section: 4.5 Final Steps for Hardness for Non-Transitive Reflexive Tournaments
nodes.statement_short: Surjective to H(i) iff surjective G' to H

nodes.name: Forward direction
nodes.statement: (Forwards.) Map the additional vertices in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ in the obvious fashion (by the ``identity'') to extend a surjective homomorphism from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_i$ so that it is surjective from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$.
nodes.section: 4.5 Final Steps for Hardness for Non-Transitive Reflexive Tournaments
nodes.statement_short: Extend by identity on padding

nodes.name: Backward direction
nodes.statement: (Backwards.) In any surjective homomorphism $s$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$, we have that $s(V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'(i))) \subseteq V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}(i))$ for $i=1,\ldots k$.
nodes.section: 4.5 Final Steps for Hardness for Non-Transitive Reflexive Tournaments
nodes.statement_short: Components map to corresponding components

nodes.name: Transitive case
nodes.statement: For the transitive case we can say that {\sc \ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}-Retraction} is in \ensuremath{\mathsf{NL}}\ from \cite{DalmauK08}, since $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ enjoys the ternary median operation as a polymorphism (this has been observed, inter alia, in \cite{larose2006taylor}). It follows of course that {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} is in \ensuremath{\mathsf{NL}}\ also.
nodes.section: 4.5 Final Steps for Hardness for Non-Transitive Reflexive Tournaments
nodes.statement_short: Median polymorphism gives NL via Dalmau-Krokhin

nodes.name: Non-transitive case
nodes.statement: The non-transitive case follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:hauptsatz}.
nodes.section: 4.5 Final Steps for Hardness for Non-Transitive Reflexive Tournaments
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 4

nodes.name: Recall self-map digraph
nodes.statement: Recall the self-map digraph $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}}$, with vertices the self-maps of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$, and an edge $(f,g) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$ between self-maps $f$ and $g$ if and only if for every edge $(x,y) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$, we have that $(f(x),g(y)) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$. In the self-map digraph, the endomorphisms are precisely the looped vertices.
nodes.section: 5 Digraphs with a most three vertices
nodes.statement_short: Endomorphisms are the loops of H^H

nodes.name: Curried homomorphism
nodes.statement: Consider the homomorphism $\varphi: \ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^n \rightarrow \ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}}$ induced by an $n+1$-ary polymorphism of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ where $n \geq 1$; suppose for a contradiction that the polymorphism depends on all its variables. Then clearly the image of $\varphi$ contains at least two elements, and at least one of these elements is not a constant map.
nodes.section: 5 Digraphs with a most three vertices
nodes.statement_short: Assume the polymorphism depends on all variables

nodes.name: Claim 0
nodes.statement: {\bf Claim 0.} {\em The only loops in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}}$ are the constant maps 1 and 2 and the identity. }
nodes.section: 5 Digraphs with a most three vertices
nodes.statement_short: Loops of H^H are constants 1, 2 and id

nodes.name: Proof of Claim 0
nodes.statement: {\em Proof of Claim 0}: let $f$ be an endomorphism of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$. Then $f$ maps loops to loops. Since $(1,2)\in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$, $f$ can either map both to 1, both to 2 , or fix both. Clearly if it fixes both $f$ is the identity. Otherwise, if $f(1)=f(2)=i$, then $(f(0),i) , (i,f(0)) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ so $f(0)=i$.
nodes.section: 5 Digraphs with a most three vertices
nodes.statement_short: Endomorphisms map loops to loops

nodes.name: Notation
nodes.statement: Without fear of confusion, we denote the constant maps by 0, 1 and 2. We denote the identity map by $id$.
nodes.section: 5 Digraphs with a most three vertices
nodes.statement_short: Name constants 0,1,2 and identity id

nodes.name: Claim 1
nodes.statement: {\bf Claim 1.} {\em (a) There are no edges in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}}$ between the identity and the constant maps; (b) if $(2,f), (f,1) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$, then $f=0$; (c) if $c$ is a constant map such that $(f,c),(c,f) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ then $f = c$. }
nodes.section: 5 Digraphs with a most three vertices
nodes.statement_short: Edge constraints near constant maps

nodes.name: Proof of Claim 1
nodes.statement: {\em Proof of Claim 1}: $(2,f) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ implies $(2,f(i)) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ for all $i$ so $f(i) \in \{0,2\}$ for all $i$. Similarly $(f,1)\in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ implies $f(i) \in \{0,1\}$ for all $i$ so (b) follows immediately. To prove (a), observe that any in- or out-neighbour of a constant cannot be surjective since no constant has in- or out-neighbourhood of size 3. For (c), argue again as we just did: $(1,f) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ means $f(i) \in \{1,2\}$ for all $i$, and $(f,1)\in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ implies $f(i) \in \{0,1\}$ for all $i$ and hence $f=1$; the proof for $c=2$ is identical.
nodes.section: 5 Digraphs with a most three vertices
nodes.statement_short: Neighbourhood arguments in H

nodes.name: Claim 2
nodes.statement: {\bf Claim 2.} {\em If $(f,id),(id,f) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ then $f = id$. }
nodes.section: 5 Digraphs with a most three vertices
nodes.statement_short: Two-way neighbours of id equal id

nodes.name: Proof of Claim 2
nodes.statement: {\em Proof of Claim 2}: Assume that $(f,id),(id,f) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$. If $i$ is a loop then $(i,i)\in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ implies $(f(i),i),(i,f(i))\in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ thus $f(i) = i$. Now $(0,1)\in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ implies $(f(0),1)\in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$, and $(2,0)\in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ implies $(2,f(0))\in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ so $f(0)=0$.
nodes.section: 5 Digraphs with a most three vertices
nodes.statement_short: Check loops and vertex 0

nodes.name: Image of the loop subdigraph W
nodes.statement: Obviously the loops of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^n$ are precisely the tuples whose coordinates belong to $\{1,2\}$. Call the subdigraph induced by these vertices $\ensuremath{\mathrm{W}}$, and notice it is weakly connected. Then the homomorphism $\varphi$ must map $\ensuremath{\mathrm{W}}$ onto a weakly connected digraph consisting of loops only. By Claim 1 (a) either (i) $\ensuremath{\mathrm{W}}$ is entirely mapped to $\{id\}$ or (ii) $\ensuremath{\mathrm{W}}$ is mapped by $\varphi$ to the set $\{1,2\}$.
nodes.section: 5 Digraphs with a most three vertices
nodes.statement_short: phi maps W to {id} or to {1,2} by Claim 1(a)

nodes.name: Extend to tuples with a 0
nodes.statement: Choose any tuple $X$ of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^n$ containing a coordinate equal to 0. Then there exist $Y, Z \in W$ such that $(X,Z), (Z,Y), (Y,X) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^n)$: indeed, let $Z$ be obtained from $X$ by replacing each 0 entry by 1, fixing all other coordinates, and let $Y$ be obtained from $X$ by replacing each 0 entry by 2, fixing all other coordinates. Thus in case (i) we get that $id = \varphi(Y), (\varphi(Y),\varphi(X)),(\varphi(X),\varphi(Z)) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ and $\varphi(Z)=id$ so by Claim 2 $\varphi$ maps all of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^n$ to $id$. In case (ii), we get that $\varphi(Y)$ and $\varphi(Z)$ belong to $\{1,2\}$; since $(\varphi(Z),\varphi(Y))\in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ we must in fact have that $(\varphi(Z),\varphi(Y))$ belongs to $\{(1,1),(1,2),(2,2)\}$; thus we get one of the following cases, namely $(1,\varphi(X)),(\varphi(X),1) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ or $(1,\varphi(X)),(\varphi(X),2) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ or $(2,\varphi(X)),(\varphi(X),2) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$. By Claim 1 (b) and (c) $\varphi(X)$ must be one of the constant maps 0, 1 or 2.
nodes.section: 5 Digraphs with a most three vertices
nodes.statement_short: Claims 1 and 2 determine phi(X) in each case

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Thus we conclude that $\varphi$ either maps all of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^n$ to $\{id\}$, in which case our polymorphism cannot depend on its first $n$ variables; or otherwise $\varphi$ maps all of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^n$ to constant maps, and then the polymorphism does not depend on its last variable, also a contradiction.
nodes.section: 5 Digraphs with a most three vertices
nodes.statement_short: Either case contradicts dependence on all variables

nodes.name: Reduce to sporadic digraphs
nodes.statement: As discussed, we only need to settle the complexity of {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction} and {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} for the digraphs depicted in Figure~\ref{fig:3digraphs}, as for all other partially reflexive digraphs of size at most $3$, {\sc List $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} is in P \cite{FederHellTucker}.
nodes.section: 5 Digraphs with a most three vertices
nodes.statement_short: Only the NP-hard List cases need treatment

nodes.name: Cases (a), (c), (d)
nodes.statement: When $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is as depicted in Figure~\ref{fig:3digraphs} (a), (c) or (d), then $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is an irreflexive semicomplete digraph with more than one cycle and it is known from \cite{Semicomplete} that {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} is \ensuremath{\mathsf{NP}}-hard, thus the same can be said for both {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction} and {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring}.
nodes.section: 5 Digraphs with a most three vertices
nodes.statement_short: Irreflexive semicomplete: NP-hard by Bang-Jensen-Hell-MacGillivray

nodes.name: Case (b)
nodes.statement: When $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is the partially reflexive tree of Figure~\ref{fig:3digraphs} (b), {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction} is known to be \ensuremath{\mathsf{NP}}-hard from \cite{pseudoforests} and {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} is known to be \ensuremath{\mathsf{NP}}-hard from \cite{GolovachPS12}.
nodes.section: 5 Digraphs with a most three vertices
nodes.statement_short: Known hardness for partially reflexive trees

nodes.name: Cases (e), (f)
nodes.statement: When $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is the reflexive tournament from Figure~\ref{fig:3digraphs} (e), the result follows from Corollary~\ref{c-main} or Lemma~\ref{prop:main1}. For the related case (f), we appeal to Lemma~\ref{lem:case-f} (finishing via Corollary~\ref{c-main}).
nodes.section: 5 Digraphs with a most three vertices
nodes.statement_short: Endo-trivial tournament and Lemma 16 with Corollary 1

nodes.name: Case (g)
nodes.statement: When $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is as depicted in Figure~\ref{fig:3digraphs} (g), membership in \ensuremath{\mathsf{P}}\ for {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction}, and therefore {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring}, follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:case-g}, in light of the recent groundbreaking proofs of \cite{FVproofBulatov,FVproofZhuk}.
nodes.section: 5 Digraphs with a most three vertices
nodes.statement_short: WNU polymorphism plus CSP dichotomy gives P
